```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}
```

# Bayesian hierarchical models {#bayesian-hierarchical}

Last week we fit mixed models by maximum likelihood; this week we go
Bayesian. This part defines what makes a model hierarchical, works
through partial pooling (the main payoff of a hierarchical model), and
then fits the drought random slope model by MCMC, first in Stan and
then in one line of `brms`.

## 1. What makes a model hierarchical? {#what-hierarchical}

A **hierarchical model** is written in layers. The data are described
conditional on some unobserved quantities, and those quantities are in
turn drawn from a probability distribution whose parameters are
estimated from the data. For the drought data used below (the
[random slope](Week12_MixedModels.html#random-slopes) example):

- **data layer:** each ring width is Normal around its own stand's regression line,
  $\text{width}_{jt} \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_a + a_j + (\mu_b + b_j)\,x_{jt},\ \sigma^2)$;
- **group layer:** the stand deviations come from one shared
  distribution, $(a_j, b_j) \sim \text{MVN}(0, G)$;
- **parameters:** $\mu_a$, $\mu_b$, $G$, and $\sigma$ are estimated (and
  in a Bayesian model, each gets a prior).

Groups are only one kind of unobserved layer. In a spatial model it is
a surface over the landscape, with nearby sites more alike than distant
ones (a Gaussian process like the one in [Gaussian processes](#gp), with
distance in place of temperature). In capture-recapture and occupancy
models it is each animal's or site's true state (alive or dead,
occupied or not), with one process describing how the state changes
(survival) and another describing what we see given the state
(detection). What these models share is a model for the data given
something we never observe directly, plus a model for that unobserved
thing.

Every model with random effects is hierarchical ("multilevel" and
"mixed" model mean the same thing). The stand intercepts and slopes do
the same job in the data layer as a fixed intercept and slope, but they
are treated as random draws from a population of stands rather than as
separate unknown constants.

A prior on its own doesn't make a model hierarchical. Compare two
Bayesian models for the drought slopes (leaving the intercepts aside).
Both give each stand its own slope $b_j$ in the data layer; they differ
in where the prior on $b_j$ comes from.

- **One layer (stand as a fixed factor):**
  $b_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)$ for each stand. We choose the prior's
  mean and SD before seeing the data. Each stand's slope is estimated
  completely separately, learning nothing from the data collected at the
  other stands. A Normal(0, 1) prior is so wide
  (slopes are about 0.25 mm per 10 cm) that S12's estimate is close to
  its own least-squares slope. The result: no 'pooling' of information!
- **Two layers (stand as a random effect):**
  $b_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_b, \tau_b)$, where the mean slope $\mu_b$
  and the among-stand SD $\tau_b$ are unknown and get priors of their
  own (hyperpriors), such as $\tau_b \sim \text{half-Normal}(0, 0.3)$ in
  the [brms fit](#brms). Now all 12 stands together tell us how
  much slopes vary. If the stands with long records have similar slopes,
  $\tau_b$ is small and S12's slope is pulled strongly toward $\mu_b$; if
  they differ a lot, $\tau_b$ is large and S12 keeps more of its own
  slope. This is the idea of [partial pooling](#partial-pooling) of information.

The data layer is the same in both models. The difference is who sets
the prior's SD. In the first model we choose it (a large SD for a vague
prior, a smaller one for a weakly informative prior). In the second,
the data estimate it, and that estimate decides how strongly each stand
is pulled toward the others.

One misconception that I had for a long time is that a hierarchical model had more than 
one probability distribution contributing to the likelihood. This isn't actually 
true: integrating out a layer can
collapse the hierarchy into one distribution. For example, a Normal random
intercept plus Normal noise gives a single multivariate Normal for all
the observations (the
[block-diagonal $V$](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#random-intercept)). 
Similarly, a Poisson count whose rate varies according to a gamma distribution
gives the [negative binomial](Week4_ProbabilityDistributions.html#compounding).
In both cases the model can be written in a layered (*conditional*)
form, with the unobserved stand effects or rates, or in a collapsed
(*marginal*) form, with those integrated out. For the same data the
two give the same likelihood and the same estimates of the shared
parameters.

So is the marginal form hierarchical? If it came from integrating out a
layer, yes: it is the same model, written a different way. `lmer()`
maximizes the marginal likelihood, and nobody would call a random
intercept model fit with `lmer()` anything but hierarchical! The
hierarchical structure is just folded into $V$: the within-stand
correlation is $\sigma_b^2 / (\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2)$, and $\sigma_b$
is still the SD of the stand effects. What makes a model hierarchical is
the claim behind it: that the data depend on unobserved quantities
(stand effects, a spatial surface or "random field" (coming up in
Week 14), true survival
states) that have their own probability model.

Capture-recapture analysis (which I work with a lot!) works the same way: its
usual likelihood sums over every alive-or-dead history an animal could
have had, which is the discrete version of integrating out a layer.

The same likelihood can also come with a different claim. A
multivariate Normal with equal correlations within stands, written
directly as correlated errors (`gls()` with `corCompSymm()`), says
nothing about stands differing and is usually called a marginal or
correlated-errors model. A negative binomial fit simply as a convenient
distribution for overdispersed counts is a one-layer model, even though
the same likelihood could be read as a Poisson count with an
unobserved, gamma-distributed rate.

In practice the layered form is usually worth writing down anyway:
it says where the extra variation and correlation come from (stands
really differ), and it is the only form that gives an estimate for each
stand, which is what partial pooling needs.


## 2. WOD: partial pooling by hand {#wod-pooling}

```{r wod-numbers, echo=FALSE}
wod_mu <- 3
wod_sb <- 0.5
wod_s <- 1
wod_n <- c(A = 4, B = 16)
wod_ybar <- c(A = 4.2, B = 4.0)
wod_w <- wod_sb^2 / (wod_sb^2 + wod_s^2 / wod_n)
wod_est <- wod_mu + wod_w * (wod_ybar - wod_mu)
```

The WOD (a short warm-up exercise) uses the estimate a random intercept
model gives each group. For group $j$, with $n_j$ observations and
mean $\bar y_j$,

$$\hat a_j = \hat\mu + w_j(\bar y_j - \hat\mu), \qquad
w_j = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2/n_j},$$

where $\hat\mu$ is the overall mean, $\sigma_b$ the SD among groups,
and $\sigma$ the SD within a group. The weight $w_j$ compares the
spread among groups with the sampling variance of the group's own mean.
(The [bonus derivation](#pooling-formula) shows where this comes from.)
The WOD applies it to the *Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis* (Bd)
infection load in two ponds. Across many ponds the mean load is
$\hat\mu =$ `r wod_mu` (log$_{10}$ zoospore equivalents per swab), ponds
differ with SD $\sigma_b =$ `r wod_sb`, and frogs within a pond differ
with SD $\sigma =$ `r wod_s`. Pond A had `r wod_n["A"]` frogs swabbed
with mean load `r wod_ybar["A"]`; pond B had `r wod_n["B"]` frogs with
mean `r wod_ybar["B"]`.

- Pond A: $\sigma^2/n = `r 1 / wod_n["A"]`$, so
  $w_A = `r wod_sb^2` / (`r wod_sb^2` + `r 1 / wod_n["A"]`) = `r wod_w["A"]`$
  and $\hat a_A = `r wod_mu` + `r wod_w["A"]` \times `r wod_ybar["A"] - wod_mu` = `r wod_est["A"]`$.
- Pond B: $\sigma^2/n = `r 1 / wod_n["B"]`$, so
  $w_B = `r wod_sb^2` / (`r wod_sb^2` + `r 1 / wod_n["B"]`) = `r wod_w["B"]`$
  and $\hat a_B = `r wod_mu` + `r wod_w["B"]` \times `r wod_ybar["B"] - wod_mu` = `r wod_est["B"]`$.

```{r wod-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=2.4}
par(mar = c(4, 7.5, 0.5, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(2.8, 4.4), ylim = c(0.5, 2.5), yaxt = "n", ylab = "",
     xlab = expression(log[10] ~ "zoospore equivalents"))
axis(2, at = 1:2, labels = c("pond B (16)", "pond A (4)"), las = 1)
abline(v = wod_mu, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
arrows(wod_ybar[c("B", "A")], 1:2, wod_est[c("B", "A")], 1:2, length = 0.08, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
points(wod_ybar[c("B", "A")], 1:2, pch = 1, cex = 1.4)
points(wod_est[c("B", "A")], 1:2, pch = 19, col = "steelblue", cex = 1.4)
text(wod_mu, 2.45, "overall mean", pos = 4, cex = 0.8, col = "grey40")
```

Pond A has the higher raw mean, but after pooling pond B has the higher
estimate. Four frogs give a noisy pond mean (sampling variance
`r 1 / wod_n["A"]`, as large as the among-pond variance
`r wod_sb^2`), so half of pond A's distance from the overall mean is
treated as noise. Sixteen frogs earn pond B most of its own mean.

Two limits are worth checking. As $n_j$ grows, $w_j \to 1$ and the group
keeps its own mean (no pooling). As $\sigma_b \to 0$, $w_j \to 0$ and
every group gets the overall mean (complete pooling).

Pulling each group's estimate toward the overall mean like this is
called **shrinkage**: the distance $\bar y_j - \mu$ shrinks by the
factor $w_j$. Groups with little data shrink the most, because their
own means are the noisiest. Extreme group means are partly luck, so
shrinking them makes the estimates less variable and, averaged over
groups, more accurate, at the cost of a little bias toward the mean.
It's the same idea as the
[ridge and lasso penalties](Week10_ModelComparison.html#regularization),
which shrink coefficients toward zero. The difference is where the
amount of shrinkage comes from: ridge regression chooses its penalty
$\lambda$ (often by cross-validation), while a random intercept model
estimates $\sigma_b$ from the data, and $\sigma_b$ sets every $w_j$
(see the [ridge bonus](#ridge-prior)).

## 3. Partial pooling {#partial-pooling}

To see partial pooling across many groups, we return to the simulated
drought-sensitivity data from
[random slopes](Week12_MixedModels.html#random-slopes): ring widths at
12 pinyon stands whose records run from 5 to 30 years. Precipitation is
in 10-cm units centered at 20 cm, so a stand's intercept is its ring
width in a 20-cm winter and its slope is the change in width per extra
10 cm.

```{r drought-data}
library(mvtnorm)
library(lme4)
set.seed(12)
n_years <- rep(c(30, 24, 18, 12, 8, 5), each = 2)        # record length per stand
tau_true <- c(0.15, 0.10)                                 # among-stand SDs: intercept, slope
rho_true <- -0.6
G_true <- diag(tau_true) %*% matrix(c(1, rho_true, rho_true, 1), 2) %*% diag(tau_true)
ab_true <- rmvnorm(12, c(0.9, 0.25), G_true)              # each stand's intercept and slope
stand_names <- sprintf("S%02d", 1:12)
drought <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, n_years)),
                      year = unlist(lapply(n_years, function(n) seq(2021 - n, 2020))))
j <- as.integer(drought$stand)
drought$precip <- round(rgamma(nrow(drought), shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1)
drought$precip10 <- (drought$precip - 20) / 10
drought$width <- round(ab_true[j, 1] + ab_true[j, 2] * drought$precip10 +
                         rnorm(nrow(drought), 0, 0.12), 2)

# no pooling: one least-squares line per stand; and the maximum likelihood random slope fit
nopool <- t(sapply(split(drought, drought$stand), function(s) coef(lm(width ~ precip10, data = s))))
fit_rs_lmer <- lmer(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
ml <- c(fixef(fit_rs_lmer), as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_rs_lmer))$sdcor)
names(ml) <- c("mu_a", "mu_b", "tau_a", "tau_b", "rho", "sigma")
round(ml, 3)
```

```{r drought-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(width ~ precip, data = drought, col = "grey60", pch = 16, cex = 0.7,
     xlab = "Winter precipitation (cm)", ylab = "Ring width (mm)")
for (s in seq_len(12)) {
  xr <- range(drought$precip10[drought$stand == stand_names[s]])
  lines(20 + 10 * xr, nopool[s, 1] + nopool[s, 2] * xr, lwd = ifelse(n_years[s] <= 8, 1, 2),
        lty = ifelse(n_years[s] <= 8, 2, 1))
}
legend("topleft", c("stand with 12-30 years", "stand with 5-8 years"), lty = 1:2, lwd = 2:1,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
plot(nopool, pch = 19, xlab = "Intercept: width at 20 cm (mm)",
     ylab = "Slope (mm per 10 cm)", cex = 1.1, xlim = range(nopool[, 1]) + c(0, 0.05))
text(nopool, labels = stand_names, pos = 4, cex = 0.7, col = "grey40")
```

Left: one least-squares line per stand. Right: each stand's own
intercept and slope, the "no pooling" estimates.

There are three ways to estimate each stand's mean ring width:

- **complete pooling:** ignore stands; every stand gets the overall mean;
- **no pooling:** estimate each stand separately (stand as a fixed
  factor);
- **partial pooling:** the random effect, a compromise between the two.

With partial pooling, each stand's mean ring width gets a prior that
is built from all the other stands: it is centered on the overall mean,
and its SD ($\sigma_b$) reflects how much stands differ from one
another. The random slope model below does the same for each stand's
slope.

Ignoring precipitation for the moment, here is the random intercept
fit, checked against the formula:

```{r pooling-check}
fit_ri0 <- lmer(width ~ 1 + (1 | stand), data = drought, REML = FALSE)
sd_ri0 <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_ri0))$sdcor          # sigma_b, sigma
ybar <- tapply(drought$width, drought$stand, mean)
n_j <- as.vector(table(drought$stand))
w <- sd_ri0[1]^2 / (sd_ri0[1]^2 + sd_ri0[2]^2 / n_j)
round(cbind(own_mean = ybar, n_j, w, formula = fixef(fit_ri0) + w * (ybar - fixef(fit_ri0)),
            lmer = coef(fit_ri0)$stand[, 1]), 3)
```

The formula matches `lmer()`'s stand estimates. Here
$\hat\sigma_b =$ `r f3(sd_ri0[1])` and $\hat\sigma =$ `r f3(sd_ri0[2])`;
the widget starts at those values. It plots each stand's own mean and
its partially pooled estimate.

```{r widget-pooling, echo=FALSE}
widget("partial_pooling.html")
```

> **Question:** Set $\sigma_b$ to 0, then drag it to 0.4. Which two
> pooling choices are these? Then compare S10 and S12: their own means
> are similar (`r f2(ybar["S10"])` and `r f2(ybar["S12"])`), but one has
> 8 years and the other 5. Which moves more toward the overall mean, and
> why?

## 4. Fitting hierarchical models by MCMC {#re-priors}

The random slope model (the layers at the
[top of this part](#bayesian-hierarchical)) pools intercepts and slopes
together. The stand deviations share one distribution,
$(a_j, b_j) \sim \text{MVN}(0, G)$, with

$$G = \begin{pmatrix} \tau_a^2 & \rho\,\tau_a\tau_b \\ \rho\,\tau_a\tau_b & \tau_b^2 \end{pmatrix}$$

where $\tau_a$ and $\tau_b$ are the among-stand SDs of the intercepts
and slopes and $\rho$ is their correlation. The `lmer()` fit in
[partial pooling](#partial-pooling) estimated these by maximum
likelihood (`ml`), integrating the stand effects out of the likelihood.

A Bayesian fit usually keeps the stand effects in the model explicitly. It puts priors on
the population-level parameters ($\mu_a$, $\mu_b$, $\tau_a$, $\tau_b$,
$\rho$, $\sigma$), and the sampler draws each stand's random intercept and
slope along with everything else. In Bayesian/MCMC fitting, the hierarchical nature 
of these models is fully front and center- that is why 'Bayesian' and 
'hierarchical' are nearly synonymous in some circles! This also makes hierarchical models much
easier to fit, which is one reason Bayesian methods are so widely used
in ecology and environmental science. Compared with maximum likelihood:

- **No integral.** The sampler draws the $a_j$ and $b_j$ instead of
  integrating them out, so a Poisson or binomial response is no harder
  than a Normal one (simple marginalization via the covariance matrix in a multivariate 
  normal is much more straightforward than integrating across the random effects for other 
  response distributions).
- **Uncertainty carries through.** Each stand's estimate reflects
  uncertainty in $\tau_a$, $\tau_b$, and $\rho$, rather than plugging in
  their best values.
- **Priors help with few groups.** A weakly informative prior keeps an
  SD off the boundary at 0 and a correlation off $\pm 1$, where
  maximum likelihood 'gave up' with four stands (see
  [Q3 here](Week12_MixedModels.html#variance-discussion)).
- **The price** is choosing priors and checking the sampler (see
  [checking chains](Week9_MCMC.html#chain-checks)).

## 5. Priors for a covariance matrix {#lkj}

The random slope model needs a prior on $G$, a 2 $\times$ 2 covariance
matrix. The usual approach splits $G$ into scales and correlations,

$$G = \begin{pmatrix} \tau_a & 0 \\ 0 & \tau_b \end{pmatrix}
\Omega
\begin{pmatrix} \tau_a & 0 \\ 0 & \tau_b \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\Omega = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \rho \\ \rho & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

and puts separate priors on each piece: a half-Normal, half-$t$, or
exponential prior on each SD $\tau$, and an **LKJ prior** on the
correlation matrix $\Omega$ (named for Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe 2009, *Journal of
Multivariate Analysis*).
Older BUGS and JAGS code often used an inverse-Wishart prior on $G$
instead, which ties the prior on the SDs to the prior on the
correlations; splitting them makes each easier to choose.

The LKJ density has one shape parameter $\eta$:

$$p(\Omega) \propto \det(\Omega)^{\eta - 1}$$

For a 2 $\times$ 2 matrix, $\det(\Omega) = 1 - \rho^2$, so
$p(\rho) \propto (1 - \rho^2)^{\eta - 1}$. With $\eta = 1$ every
correlation is equally likely; $\eta > 1$ favors correlations near 0,
and $\eta < 1$ favors correlations near $\pm 1$. For a bigger matrix
($K \times K$), each single correlation has the marginal prior
$(\rho + 1)/2 \sim \text{Beta}(\eta - 1 + K/2,\ \eta - 1 + K/2)$.

```{r widget-lkj, echo=FALSE}
widget("lkj_prior.html")
```

> **Question:** For a 10 $\times$ 10 correlation matrix with $\eta = 1$,
> how likely is any one correlation to exceed 0.5 in absolute value?
> What does "uniform" mean for a matrix that large?

## 6. The random slope model in brms {#brms}

`brms` writes and runs the Stan program for a model given as an
`lme4`-style formula. Priors go in the `prior` argument, one
`prior()` call per group of parameters, combined with `c()`. Each call
names a distribution in Stan's syntax and a `class`: `b` for
fixed-effect slopes, `Intercept`, `sd` for the among-group SDs, `cor`
for their correlations, and `sigma` for the residual SD. A `coef` or
`group` argument narrows a prior to one parameter or one grouping
factor. `brms` already bounds SDs at zero, so `normal(0, 0.3)` on class
`sd` is a half-Normal. `get_prior(formula, data)` lists every
parameter that can take a prior, with its default.

The order of the `prior()` calls does not matter. `brms` matches each
one to parameters by its `class`, `coef`, and `group`, not by its
position. When two priors could apply to the same parameter, the more
specific one wins wherever it sits in the list: a prior with
`coef = "precip10"` overrides a class-wide `b` prior. Giving the same
parameter two priors at the same level is an error.

Here is the random slope model with Normal priors on the mean
intercept and slope, half-Normal(0, 0.3) priors on the among-stand SDs
and on $\sigma$, and an LKJ(2) prior on the correlation. Mean ring width
is around 1 mm, so Normal(1, 0.5) on the intercept rules out
implausible values (a mean width of 3 mm, or a negative one) but is
otherwise vague; Normal(0, 0.5) on the slope allows a change of up to
about 1 mm per 10 cm of precipitation in either direction. 
One detail: `brms` puts the `Intercept` prior on the
intercept at the *sample mean* of each predictor, not at zero. Here the
mean of `precip10` is `r round(mean(drought$precip10), 2)`, so the two
are close.

```{r brms-fit, cache=TRUE, results="hide"}
library(brms)
fit_brms <- brm(width ~ precip10 + (precip10 | stand), data = drought,
                prior = c(prior(normal(1, 0.5), class = Intercept),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.5), class = b),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = sd),
                          prior(lkj(2), class = cor),
                          prior(normal(0, 0.3), class = sigma)),
                backend = "cmdstanr", chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0)
```

Check the sampler first (no divergent transitions, $\hat R$ near 1,
large effective sample sizes; see
[checking chains](Week9_MCMC.html#chain-checks)), then the estimates:

```{r brms-summary}
summary(fit_brms)
```

`prior_summary(fit_brms)` lists every prior in a fit. Without the
`prior` argument, `brms` uses an LKJ(1) prior on the correlations and
half-Student-$t$ priors on the SDs. `rstanarm::stan_lmer()` fits the
same formula from precompiled models, so it skips the compile step.

```{r brms-numbers, echo=FALSE}
library(posterior)
draws <- as_draws_df(fit_brms)
q <- function(v) quantile(v, c(0.5, 0.05, 0.95))
post <- rbind(mu_a = q(draws$b_Intercept), mu_b = q(draws$b_precip10),
              tau_a = q(draws$sd_stand__Intercept), tau_b = q(draws$sd_stand__precip10),
              rho = q(draws$cor_stand__Intercept__precip10), sigma = q(draws$sigma))
ml_vs_bayes <- data.frame(truth = c(0.9, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, -0.6, 0.12),
                          lmer = ml, post)
names(ml_vs_bayes)[3:5] <- c("posterior median", "5%", "95%")
ab_post <- coef(fit_brms)$stand[, "Estimate", ]          # posterior means, one row per stand
err <- function(est, rows = 1:12) colMeans(abs(est[rows, ] - ab_true[rows, ]))
short_rows <- which(n_years <= 8)
err_nopool_short <- err(nopool, short_rows)
err_post_short <- err(ab_post, short_rows)
```

```{r ml-bayes-table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(ml_vs_bayes, digits = 3, caption = "Maximum likelihood (lmer) and posterior summaries")
```

The two methods agree closely on everything except the correlation: the
MLE is `r f2(ml["rho"])`, while the posterior median is
`r f2(post["rho", 1])` with a 90% interval from `r f2(post["rho", 2])`
to `r f2(post["rho", 3])`.

```{r rho-posterior, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.6}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
hist(draws$cor_stand__Intercept__precip10, breaks = 40, freq = FALSE, col = "grey85", border = "white", xlim = c(-1, 1),
     main = "", xlab = expression(rho ~ "(intercept-slope correlation)"))
curve(dbeta((x + 1) / 2, 2, 2) / 2, add = TRUE, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = ml["rho"], lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
abline(v = -0.6, lwd = 2, lty = 3)
legend("topright", c("LKJ(2) prior", "MLE (lmer)", "truth"), lty = c(2, 1, 3), lwd = 2,
       col = c("black", "firebrick", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

```{r shrinkage-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(nopool, pch = 1, cex = 1.2, xlab = "Intercept: width at 20 cm (mm)",
     ylab = "Slope (mm per 10 cm)",
     xlim = range(nopool[, 1], ab_post[, 1]) + c(0, 0.06), ylim = range(nopool[, 2], ab_post[, 2]))
arrows(nopool[, 1], nopool[, 2], ab_post[, 1], ab_post[, 2], length = 0.07, col = "steelblue")
points(ab_post, pch = 19, col = "steelblue")
text(nopool, labels = paste0(stand_names, " (", n_years, ")"), pos = 4, cex = 0.65, col = "grey40")
points(post["mu_a", 1], post["mu_b", 1], pch = 3, cex = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("own least-squares fit", "posterior mean", "population mean"),
       pch = c(1, 19, 3), col = c("black", "steelblue", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

Each arrow runs from a stand's own fit to its posterior mean; the
number in parentheses is the record length. Stands with short records
move the most; stands with 24 or 30 years barely move.

```{r shrink-sims, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(746)
shrink_sims <- t(replicate(500, {
  ab <- rmvnorm(12, c(0.9, 0.25), G_true)
  sim <- data.frame(stand = factor(rep(stand_names, n_years)))
  k <- as.integer(sim$stand)
  sim$x <- (round(rgamma(nrow(sim), shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1) - 20) / 10
  sim$y <- ab[k, 1] + ab[k, 2] * sim$x + rnorm(nrow(sim), 0, 0.12)
  np <- t(sapply(split(sim, sim$stand), function(s) coef(lm(y ~ x, data = s))))
  pp <- as.matrix(coef(lmer(y ~ x + (x | stand), data = sim, REML = FALSE))$stand)
  sh <- n_years <= 8
  c(np_a = mean(abs(np - ab)[sh, 1]), np_b = mean(abs(np - ab)[sh, 2]),
    pp_a = mean(abs(pp - ab)[sh, 1]), pp_b = mean(abs(pp - ab)[sh, 2]))
}))
```

Because the data are simulated, we can compare both sets of estimates
with the true stand values. For the four stands with 5 or 8 years, the
average error in the slopes is `r f3(err_nopool_short[2])` mm per 10 cm
with no pooling and `r f3(err_post_short[2])` with partial pooling
(intercepts: `r f3(err_nopool_short[1])` and `r f3(err_post_short[1])`
mm). That's a mixed result: in any one data set, shrinkage can pull a
stand that really is unusual too far toward the mean. Its advantage is
on average. Over `r nrow(shrink_sims)` simulated data sets with the same
design, using `lmer()`'s stand estimates, partial pooling cut the
average slope error for the short-record stands from
`r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "np_b"]))` to `r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "pp_b"]))`
(intercepts: `r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "np_a"]))` to
`r f3(mean(shrink_sims[, "pp_a"]))`).

> **Question:** Why is the posterior for $\rho$ so much wider than the
> other posteriors, and why is its median closer to 0 than the MLE?
> Which summary is more honest about what 12 stands can tell us?

> **Question:** Change `lkj(2)` to `lkj(1)`, then to `lkj(10)`, and
> refit. Predict how the posterior for $\rho$ will move before you run
> each one. Do the stand estimates change much?

## Discussion {#bayes-discussion}

**Q1.** With 12 stands, the 90% interval for $\rho$ runs from
`r f2(post["rho", 2])` to `r f2(post["rho", 3])`. To rule out
$\rho = 0$, would you rather have 12 more stands or 20 more years at
each of the 12 stands? Defend your choice.

**Q2.** When would you use `brms`, and when would you write the Stan
model yourself (as in the [Stan bonus](#stan-model))?

**Q3.** Do your final project data have groups (sites, individuals,
years, observers)? Which effects would you treat as random, and would
you let any slopes vary among groups?

## Bonus: where the partial pooling formula comes from {#pooling-formula}

Take the simplest hierarchical model, a random intercept with no
covariates. Observation $i$ in group $j$ is

$$y_{ij} = \mu + a_j + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad
a_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_b^2), \qquad
\varepsilon_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2),$$

and group $j$ has $n_j$ observations with mean $\bar y_j$. Write
$\theta_j = \mu + a_j$ for the group's true mean. For now, treat $\mu$,
$\sigma_b$, and $\sigma$ as known. Two sources of information bear on
$\theta_j$:

- **the group's own data:** each $y_{ij} \sim \text{Normal}(\theta_j, \sigma^2)$;
- **the other groups:** the group layer says
  $\theta_j \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma_b^2)$, which acts as a prior.

Multiply the two and take the log. Dropping terms that don't involve
$\theta_j$,

$$\log p(\theta_j \mid \text{data}) =
-\sum_{i=1}^{n_j} \frac{(y_{ij} - \theta_j)^2}{2\sigma^2}
- \frac{(\theta_j - \mu)^2}{2\sigma_b^2} + \text{constant}$$

To find the best estimate, set the derivative with respect to
$\theta_j$ to zero. Since $\sum_i (y_{ij} - \theta_j) = n_j(\bar y_j - \theta_j)$,

$$\frac{n_j(\bar y_j - \theta_j)}{\sigma^2} - \frac{\theta_j - \mu}{\sigma_b^2} = 0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat\theta_j = \frac{(n_j/\sigma^2)\,\bar y_j + (1/\sigma_b^2)\,\mu}{n_j/\sigma^2 + 1/\sigma_b^2}$$

This is a weighted average of the group's own mean and the overall
mean, each weighted by its precision (1/variance): $\bar y_j$ has
variance $\sigma^2/n_j$, and the group layer has variance
$\sigma_b^2$. Rearranging (multiply the top and bottom by
$\sigma_b^2\sigma^2/n_j$) gives the form used in the [WOD](#wod-pooling)
(where $\hat\theta_j$ is written $\hat a_j$),

$$\hat\theta_j = \mu + w_j(\bar y_j - \mu), \qquad
w_j = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2/n_j}.$$

Because the posterior here is Normal, $\hat\theta_j$ is both its mode
and its mean. A maximum likelihood fit like `lmer()` uses the same
formula, with estimates of $\mu$, $\sigma_b$, and $\sigma$ plugged in.

## Bonus: the same model written in Stan {#stan-model}

Writing the Stan program yourself shows what `brms` does behind the
scenes, and it is the starting point for models no formula can express
(nonlinear functions, latent states, observation models). The program
below is the random slope model with the same priors as the
[brms fit](#brms).
Two choices in it need explaining.

- **The Cholesky factor.** Stan works with $L$, the lower-triangular
  matrix with $LL^T = \Omega$. Any value Stan proposes for
  `cholesky_factor_corr` gives a valid correlation matrix, so the
  sampler can't leave the allowed region (the third problem in
  [why these models are harder to fit](Week12_MixedModels.html#harder)),
  and it's cheaper to compute with.
- **Non-centered stand effects.** Instead of sampling $(a_j, b_j)$
  directly, Stan samples standard Normal $z_j$ and computes
  $(a_j, b_j)^T = \text{diag}(\tau)\,L\,z_j$. This avoids the funnel
  that makes hierarchical models hard to sample
  ([when HMC struggles](Week9_MCMC.html#hmc-failures)).

```{r stan-fit, cache=TRUE, echo=-6, results="hide"}
library(cmdstanr)
slopes_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;                       // stand-years
  int<lower=1> J;                       // stands
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=J> stand;
  vector[N] x;                          // precipitation (10 cm, centered at 20 cm)
  vector[N] y;                          // ring width (mm)
}
parameters {
  vector[2] mu;                         // mean intercept and slope
  vector<lower=0>[2] tau;               // among-stand SDs of intercepts and slopes
  cholesky_factor_corr[2] L;            // Cholesky factor of the correlation matrix
  matrix[2, J] z;                       // standardized stand effects
  real<lower=0> sigma;                  // residual SD
}
transformed parameters {
  // row j: stand j's intercept and slope
  matrix[J, 2] ab = rep_matrix(mu', J) + (diag_pre_multiply(tau, L) * z)';
}
model {
  mu[1] ~ normal(1, 0.5);
  mu[2] ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  tau ~ normal(0, 0.3);                 // half-normal, because tau > 0
  L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(z) ~ std_normal();
  sigma ~ normal(0, 0.3);
  y ~ normal(ab[stand, 1] + ab[stand, 2] .* x, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real rho = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L)[1, 2];
}
"
slopes_model <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(slopes_code))
stan_data <- list(N = nrow(drought), J = 12, stand = as.integer(drought$stand),
                  x = drought$precip10, y = drought$width)
fit_stan <- slopes_model$sample(data = stan_data, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4,
                                seed = 746, refresh = 0)
fit_stan$draws()
```

Check the sampler first, then the estimates:

```{r stan-check}
fit_stan$diagnostic_summary()
fit_stan$summary(c("mu", "tau", "rho", "sigma"))
```

The estimates match the `brms` fit up to Monte Carlo error.
`stancode(fit_brms)` prints the program `brms` wrote; it uses the same
Cholesky factor and non-centered stand effects.

## Bonus: ridge regression as a prior {#ridge-prior}

A [ridge penalty](Week10_ModelComparison.html#regularization) adds
$\lambda\sum\beta_k^2$ to the NLL. A Normal(0, $\tau^2$) prior on each
$\beta_k$ adds $-\log p(\beta) = \sum\beta_k^2/(2\tau^2)$ plus a
constant, which is the same penalty with $\lambda = 1/(2\tau^2)$; a
Laplace prior gives the lasso (see
[Bayesian model comparison and shrinkage priors](Week10_ModelComparison.html#bayesian)).
A random effect puts the same kind of penalty on the stand deviations:
the $\text{MVN}(0, G)$ prior shrinks every $(a_j, b_j)$ toward 0, with
$G$ estimated rather than chosen. The [wiggliness penalty](#penalty) on
a spline works the same way.

# Splines, GAMs, and Gaussian processes {#gams}

When no function from the bestiary has the right shape, we can build
one out of simple pieces. A spline is a weighted sum of basis
functions, so fitting it is a linear model; a penalty on wiggliness
keeps it from chasing noise, and that penalty is a prior, which makes
the smooth a kind of random effect. A Gaussian process skips the basis
functions and puts a multivariate Normal directly on the curve, using a
covariance matrix like the ones built for
[autocorrelation](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1).

## 1. A thermal performance curve {#thermal}

```{r workflow-models, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("MODELS")
```

The chytrid fungus Bd grows fastest at moderate temperatures and dies
when it gets too warm, which is one reason warm ponds have less
infection. A management question: **above what water temperature does
Bd stop growing?** To find out, we grow 48 Bd cultures on a thermal
gradient plate (a block heated at one end and cooled at the other), so
each culture sits at a slightly different temperature, and estimate each
culture's growth rate $r$ (per day) from a week of optical density
readings. These data are simulated; the curve they came from is in the
code below, and none of the models on this page has that form.

```{r bd-data}
# truth: a two-piece thermal performance curve (Gaussian rise, quadratic fall)
tpc_true <- function(temp) 0.3 * ifelse(temp <= 20, exp(-((temp - 20) / 8)^2), 1 - ((temp - 20) / 8)^2)
set.seed(13)
bd <- data.frame(temp = round(seq(4, 29, length.out = 48) + runif(48, -0.2, 0.2), 1))
bd$r <- round(tpc_true(bd$temp) + rnorm(48, 0, 0.03), 3)
head(bd)
```

Thermal performance curves are usually asymmetric: a slow rise, an
optimum $T_\text{opt}$, then a steep fall to a critical maximum
$\text{CT}_\text{max}$ where growth stops. A first try from the
bestiary is a Gaussian (bell) curve, with a peak height, a location
($T_\text{opt}$), and a width, fit by maximum likelihood with Normal
noise:

```{r bell-fit}
bell <- function(temp, rmax, topt, width) rmax * exp(-(temp - topt)^2 / (2 * width^2))
nll_bell <- function(par) {
  -sum(dnorm(bd$r, bell(bd$temp, par[1], par[2], par[3]), exp(par[4]), log = TRUE))
}
fit_bell <- optim(c(0.3, 20, 5, log(0.05)), nll_bell)
round(setNames(c(fit_bell$par[1:3], exp(fit_bell$par[4])), c("rmax", "topt", "width", "sigma")), 3)
```

```{r bell-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot_bd()
curve(bell(x, fit_bell$par[1], fit_bell$par[2], fit_bell$par[3]), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("topleft", "Gaussian (bell) fit", lwd = 2, col = "firebrick", bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

> **Question:** Which features of the scatter does the bell curve get
> wrong? Which of them matter for the management question?

## 2. Splines are linear models {#basis}

A spline builds a curve from $K$ fixed **basis functions**
$B_1(x), \dots, B_K(x)$ and estimated weights:

$$f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k B_k(x)$$

The basis functions are chosen in advance, so the only unknowns are the
weights, and $f$ is linear in them. That makes the spline a linear
model: each basis function becomes one column of the
[model matrix](Week11_LinearModelsAndVariance.html#linear-algebra), and
`lm()` estimates the weights.

The most common basis is the **B-spline**. Each cubic B-spline is a
small bump built from cubic pieces that join smoothly at points called
**knots**, and it is zero outside a short stretch of $x$. More knots
mean more, narrower bumps and a more flexible curve. In R,
`splines::bs()` builds the columns:

```{r bs-basis}
library(splines)
X <- bs(bd$temp, df = 6)          # 6 cubic B-spline columns (3 interior knots)
round(head(X), 3)
attr(X, "knots")
fit_bs6 <- lm(r ~ bs(temp, df = 6), data = bd)
fit_bs25 <- lm(r ~ bs(temp, df = 25), data = bd)
```

```{r bs-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.8}
temp_grid <- seq(4, 29, by = 0.05)
Xg <- predict(X, temp_grid)
pal <- c("#2a78d6", "#c0392b", "#27ae60", "#8e44ad", "#d68910", "black")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1.5, 1))
matplot(temp_grid, Xg, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = pal, xlab = "Temperature (°C)",
        ylab = "Basis function value", main = "Six B-spline basis functions", cex.main = 0.9)
abline(v = attr(X, "knots"), lty = 3, col = "grey50")
plot_bd(main = "Unpenalized spline fits", cex.main = 0.9)
lines(temp_grid, predict(fit_bs6, data.frame(temp = temp_grid)), lwd = 2.5, col = "#2a78d6")
lines(temp_grid, predict(fit_bs25, data.frame(temp = temp_grid)), lwd = 1.5, col = "black", lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("6 basis functions", "25 basis functions"), lwd = c(2.5, 1.5), lty = 1:2,
       col = c("#2a78d6", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The six-function fit (left: its basis functions, with dotted lines at
the knots) has the right shape. With 25 basis functions, the curve
starts chasing individual cultures, the same problem as the
[connect-the-dots curve](Week10_ModelComparison.html#wod) that passes
through every point.

Other bases work the same way. The widget builds $f(x)$ from four kinds
of basis functions and random weights. Polynomials ($1, x, x^2, \dots$)
are the oldest choice, but each power stretches across the whole range,
so changing one weight moves the curve everywhere. B-splines and
Gaussian bumps are local: each weight changes the curve over one stretch
of $x$.

```{r widget-basis, echo=FALSE}
widget("spline_basis.html")
```

> **Question:** With B-splines of degree 1 and 4 interior knots, where
> can the function bend? Switch to degree 3 and compare. Then choose the
> polynomial basis with highest power 12 and randomize a few times:
> where does the function do most of its moving?

> **Question:** Switch the weights to a random walk and lower the step
> SD. What happens to the function, and what would you have to assume
> about the weights to get a smooth curve from many knots?

## 3. Penalizing wiggliness {#penalty}

Choosing the number of knots by hand is awkward: too few and the curve
can't bend where it needs to, too many and it chases noise. The usual
fix is to use plenty of basis functions and add a **penalty** to the
NLL that grows with how wiggly the curve is:

$$\text{NLL}_\text{pen}(\beta) = \text{NLL}(\beta) +
\lambda \sum_{k=3}^{K} (\beta_k - 2\beta_{k-1} + \beta_{k-2})^2$$

The penalty adds up squared second differences of neighboring weights,
a stand-in for the curvature of $f$ (the integral of $f''(x)^2$ is
the other common choice). With $\lambda = 0$ we get the unpenalized
`lm()` fit. As $\lambda$ grows, the weights are forced onto a straight
line, and with evenly spaced knots so is $f$. In between, the **effective degrees of freedom**
(edf) measure how many parameters' worth of flexibility the curve uses;
edf runs from $K$ (no penalty) down to 2 (a straight line).

Choosing $\lambda$ is the remaining problem.
[Cross-validation](Week10_ModelComparison.html#cross-validation) would
work, but there's a faster route, because **the penalty is a prior.**
As in the [ridge bonus](#ridge-prior), a penalty $\lambda \sum d_k^2$
on the second differences $d_k$ is what a Normal(0, $\tau^2$) prior on
each $d_k$ adds to the NLL, with $\lambda = 1/(2\tau^2)$. Read that
way, the wiggly part of the curve is a random effect: a set of
deviations drawn from a Normal distribution whose SD $\tau$ is
estimated from the data. So $\lambda$ can be chosen the way `lmer()`
estimates $\sigma_b$, by maximizing the restricted likelihood (REML)
with the weights integrated out.

The widget fits the Bd data with a P-spline (cubic B-splines on evenly
spaced knots, plus the second-difference penalty) and plots the REML
criterion against $\lambda$.

```{r widget-penalty, echo=FALSE}
widget("penalized_fit.html")
```

> **Question:** Start at 40 basis functions and $\log_{10}\lambda = -4$,
> then raise $\lambda$. What happens to edf, and why does the curve end
> up a sloped line rather than a flat one? Then press "Jump to the REML
> minimum" and try 10, 20, and 40 basis functions. How much does $K$
> matter once $\lambda$ is chosen this way?

## 4. Fitting a GAM {#gam}

A **generalized additive model** (GAM) is a GLM in which some terms are
smooth functions like this one:
$g(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + f_1(x_{1i}) + f_2(x_{2i}) + \dots$, with any link
$g$ and response distribution. `mgcv::gam()` takes `s()` terms in an
ordinary model formula:

```{r gam-fit}
library(mgcv)
fit_gam <- gam(r ~ s(temp, k = 20), data = bd, method = "REML")
summary(fit_gam)
gam.vcomp(fit_gam)          # the smooth's SD, printed like a variance component
```

```{r gam-gcv, echo=FALSE}
edf_gcv <- sum(gam(r ~ s(temp, k = 20), data = bd)$edf) - 1
```

`k = 20` sets the number of basis functions, an upper limit on
flexibility; the penalty decides how much of it to use (edf
`r f1(sum(fit_gam$edf) - 1)` here). Ask for `method = "REML"`:
`gam()`'s default, generalized cross-validation, tends to pick wigglier
curves (edf `r f1(edf_gcv)` for these data). `gam()`'s default basis is a thin
plate regression spline, which works like the B-splines above;
`s(temp, bs = "ps")` asks for the P-spline from the widget instead. For
counts, use `family = poisson` as in `glm()`.

```{r compare-fits, echo=FALSE}
aic_tab <- data.frame(
  model = c("Gaussian (bell)", "B-spline, 6 basis functions (lm)", "Penalized spline (gam, REML)"),
  parameters = c(4, length(coef(fit_bs6)) + 1, sum(fit_gam$edf) + 1),
  logLik = c(-fit_bell$value, logLik(fit_bs6), logLik(fit_gam)),
  AIC = c(2 * fit_bell$value + 8, AIC(fit_bs6), AIC(fit_gam)))
aic_tab$dAIC <- aic_tab$AIC - min(aic_tab$AIC)
knitr::kable(aic_tab, digits = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 1), col.names = c("Model", "Parameters (edf)",
             "logLik", "AIC", "$\\Delta$AIC"))
```

```{r gam-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.2}
pg <- predict(fit_gam, data.frame(temp = temp_grid), se.fit = TRUE)
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot_bd()
polygon(c(temp_grid, rev(temp_grid)), c(pg$fit + 1.96 * pg$se.fit, rev(pg$fit - 1.96 * pg$se.fit)),
        col = adjustcolor("#2a78d6", 0.2), border = NA)
lines(temp_grid, pg$fit, lwd = 2.5, col = "#2a78d6")
curve(bell(x, fit_bell$par[1], fit_bell$par[2], fit_bell$par[3]), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("GAM with 95% interval", "Gaussian (bell)"), lwd = 2, lty = 1:2,
       col = c("#2a78d6", "firebrick"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
topt_gam <- temp_grid[which.max(pg$fit)]
ctmax_gam <- temp_grid[temp_grid > topt_gam & pg$fit < 0][1]
```

The GAM finds the steep fall the bell can't make. Its curve peaks at
`r f1(topt_gam)` °C and crosses zero at `r f1(ctmax_gam)` °C; the
bell puts the peak at `r f1(fit_bell$par[2])` °C and never reaches
zero. (AIC for a GAM uses the edf as its parameter count; it's a
reasonable guide, not an exact one, since $\lambda$ was itself
estimated.)

## 5. Gaussian processes {#gp}

A spline puts a prior on basis-function weights. A **Gaussian process**
(GP) puts a prior directly on the curve: the values of $f$ at any set
of temperatures are multivariate Normal,

$$f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n) \sim \text{MVN}(m\mathbf{1}, K), \qquad
K_{ij} = \alpha^2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x_i - x_j)^2}{2\ell^2}\right)$$

The **kernel** $K_{ij}$ says that cultures at similar temperatures have
similar growth rates: the correlation falls from 1 to near 0 as the
temperature gap grows past a few **length-scales** $\ell$. The amplitude
$\alpha$ sets how far $f$ wanders from its mean $m$. This kernel (the
squared exponential) gives very smooth curves. The exponential kernel,
$\exp(-|x_i - x_j|/\ell)$, gives rough ones, and for equally spaced
times it is the
[AR(1) correlation](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1) $\rho^{|s-t|}$ with
$\rho = e^{-1/\ell}$.

Adding Normal measurement noise gives
$y \sim \text{MVN}(m\mathbf{1}, K + \sigma^2 I)$, so the likelihood is
one multivariate Normal density, with four parameters ($m$, $\alpha$,
$\ell$, $\sigma$) to fit by `optim()`:

```{r gp-fit}
dist_temp <- abs(outer(bd$temp, bd$temp, "-"))
nll_gp <- function(par) {
  m <- par[1]
  alpha <- exp(par[2])
  ell <- exp(par[3])
  sigma <- exp(par[4])
  V <- alpha^2 * exp(-dist_temp^2 / (2 * ell^2)) + sigma^2 * diag(nrow(bd))
  -dmvnorm(bd$r, rep(m, nrow(bd)), V, log = TRUE)
}
fit_gp <- optim(c(0.15, log(0.15), log(4), log(0.03)), nll_gp, method = "BFGS")
gp_par <- c(m = fit_gp$par[1], exp(fit_gp$par[2:4]))
names(gp_par) <- c("m", "alpha", "ell", "sigma")
round(gp_par, 3)
```

The length-scale is long compared with the 25-degree range of the
data, so the curve is one broad excursion from $m$, and $m$ trades off
against $\alpha$; don't read much into its value.

The prediction at a new temperature $x^*$ is the conditional mean of
$f(x^*)$ given the data, from the same MVN rules:
$\hat f(x^*) = m + k_*^T (K + \sigma^2 I)^{-1}(y - m\mathbf{1})$, where
$k_*$ holds the covariances between $f(x^*)$ and the observed cultures.

```{r gp-predict}
gp_predict <- function(new_temp, p = gp_par) {
  K <- p["alpha"]^2 * exp(-dist_temp^2 / (2 * p["ell"]^2)) + p["sigma"]^2 * diag(nrow(bd))
  k_star <- p["alpha"]^2 * exp(-outer(new_temp, bd$temp, "-")^2 / (2 * p["ell"]^2))
  as.vector(p["m"] + k_star %*% solve(K, bd$r - p["m"]))
}
gp_fit_grid <- gp_predict(temp_grid)
max(abs(gp_fit_grid - pg$fit))          # largest gap between the GP and GAM curves
```

```{r gp-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot_bd()
lines(temp_grid, pg$fit, lwd = 3, col = "#2a78d6")
lines(temp_grid, gp_fit_grid, lwd = 2, col = "black", lty = 2)
legend("topleft", c("GAM", "Gaussian process"), lwd = c(3, 2), lty = 1:2,
       col = c("#2a78d6", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
```

The GP and the GAM give nearly the same curve, with length-scale
$\hat\ell =$ `r f1(gp_par["ell"])` °C. That's no accident: a penalized
spline and a GP are both a smooth curve with a multivariate Normal
prior, one written through basis weights and the other through a kernel.

In the widget, choose a kernel and length-scale, draw random curves from
the prior, then click to add observations and see the posterior.

```{r widget-gp, echo=FALSE}
widget("gp_draws.html")
```

> **Question:** Add the example points. Switch the kernel from squared
> exponential to exponential. What changes about the curves between the
> observations? Then shrink $\ell$ to 0.3: what does the posterior do
> far from any observation?

The $x$ in a GP can be anything with a distance: temperature, time, or
position. Replace $|x_i - x_j|$ with the distance between two sampling
sites and the same kernel describes how similar nearby sites are, which
is the core of spatial regression models (in geostatistics, prediction
from this model is called kriging).

## Discussion {#gam-discussion}

```{r extrapolation, echo=FALSE}
ext <- c(bell = bell(32, fit_bell$par[1], fit_bell$par[2], fit_bell$par[3]),
         gam = as.vector(predict(fit_gam, data.frame(temp = 32))),
         gp = gp_predict(32))
```

**Q1.** At 32 °C, outside the plate's range, the bell predicts a growth
rate of `r f3(ext["bell"])` per day, the GAM `r f3(ext["gam"])`, and
the GP `r f3(ext["gp"])`. Why do they disagree, and which (if any) would
you use to say whether Bd survives in a 32 °C pond?

**Q2.** The GAM beats the bell by `r f1(aic_tab$dAIC[1])` AIC units. A
colleague concludes that "Bd's thermal performance curve is
asymmetric." What has the comparison corroborated, and what hasn't it?
What parametric rival would you add?

**Q3.** A manager wants one number: the temperature at which Bd stops
growing, with an interval. The bell has a parameter for $T_\text{opt}$;
the GAM has no parameter for anything. Which model would you report
from, and how?

## Bonus: uncertainty in derived quantities {#derived}

$T_\text{opt}$ and $\text{CT}_\text{max}$ aren't parameters of the GAM,
but they are functions of its weights. `gam()` returns an approximate
posterior for the weights (MVN, with covariance `vcov(fit_gam)`), so we
can draw many sets of weights, compute both quantities for each curve,
and summarize:

```{r derived}
Xp <- predict(fit_gam, data.frame(temp = temp_grid), type = "lpmatrix")   # basis at each grid point
set.seed(746)
beta_sims <- rmvnorm(2000, coef(fit_gam), vcov(fit_gam))
curves <- Xp %*% t(beta_sims)                                              # one column per curve
topt_sims <- temp_grid[apply(curves, 2, which.max)]
ctmax_sims <- apply(curves, 2, function(f) {
  above <- temp_grid > 20 & f < 0
  if (any(above)) temp_grid[which(above)[1]] else NA
})
round(rbind(topt = quantile(topt_sims, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975)),
            ctmax = quantile(ctmax_sims, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)), 1)
```

The true curve peaks at 20 °C and reaches zero at 28 °C.

## Bonus: a smooth in brms {#smooth-brms}

`brms` accepts `mgcv`'s `s()` terms and fits them as random effects,
which makes the [penalty-as-prior](#penalty) idea concrete:

```{r brms-gam, cache=TRUE, results="hide"}
fit_brms_gam <- brm(r ~ s(temp, k = 20), data = bd, backend = "cmdstanr",
                    chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 746, refresh = 0,
                    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95))
```

```{r brms-gam-summary}
summary(fit_brms_gam)
```

The `sds(stemp_1)` line is the SD of the smooth's wiggly part (the
$\tau$ above), on a different scale from `gam.vcomp()`'s because the
two packages scale the basis functions differently. In
`stancode(fit_brms_gam)`, the wiggly weights are
standard Normal draws multiplied by that SD, the same non-centered form
as the [random slopes in Stan](#stan-model).

## Bonus: GAMs with more terms {#gam-terms}

Smooths combine with everything else in a model formula. Some forms
that come up in ecological data:

| `mgcv` formula | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| `y ~ s(x1) + s(x2) + x3` | two smooth effects and a linear one, added together |
| `y ~ f + s(x, by = f)` | a separate smooth of `x` for each level of factor `f` |
| `y ~ s(x) + s(g, bs = "re")` | a smooth plus a random intercept for group `g` |
| `y ~ s(x) + s(x, g, bs = "fs")` | a shared smooth plus group-level smooths, shrunk toward it |
| `y ~ te(x1, x2)` | a smooth surface in two variables (for example, a temperature-by-moisture response) |
| `y ~ s(lon, lat)` | a smooth surface over space |

Pedersen et al. (2019, *PeerJ* 7: e6876) describe these hierarchical
GAMs and when to use each, with ecological examples.
